etymology: The name of the Swiss city that became, under Calvin, the chief center of the Reformed Reformation; from the Latin Genava.
biblical_def: Geneva is the Swiss city that became, under the ministry of John Calvin, the chief center and model of the Reformed Reformation, called by John Knox “the most perfect school of Christ that ever was in the earth since the days of the apostles.” Having embraced the Reformation in 1536, the city received Calvin, who—apart from a period of exile—labored there until his death in 1564, preaching through the Scriptures, ordering the church after the New Testament pattern of pastors, teachers, elders, and deacons, establishing the Academy that trained ministers for all of Europe, and shaping the city’s life by the Word of God. From Geneva the Reformed faith went out across the continent and the British Isles: Knox carried it to Scotland, the Marian exiles brought it home to England, and the Huguenots, the Dutch, and others looked to Geneva as their mother. There the Geneva Bible was produced, the English Scriptures that the Pilgrims and Puritans carried to the New World; there Calvin’s Institutes and commentaries were written and printed. The dictionary honors Geneva as the great seedbed of Reformed Christianity, while remembering that Calvin himself pointed away from the city and the man to Christ and the Word. Geneva was not a perfect city nor Calvin a perfect man, and its civil arrangements belonged to its age; but as a center from which the recovered gospel of grace and a Scripture-ordered church spread through the world, Geneva holds an honored place in the history of the church.
webster_summary: The Swiss city that became, under Calvin, the chief center of the Reformed Reformation—home of the Academy and the Geneva Bible, from which the Reformed faith spread across Europe and Britain.

corruption_summary: Geneva is caricatured as a grim theocratic tyranny, or idolized as a perfect model, missing its true place as a seedbed of the recovered gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Geneva’s true significance as a center from which the recovered gospel and a Scripture-ordered church spread through the world. The common caricature paints Geneva as a grim theocratic tyranny and Calvin as its dictator, fixing on the civil severities of the age while ignoring the preaching, the Academy, the care of the poor, and the missionary outflow that made the city a light. The dictionary corrects the caricature without idolizing the city.

For Geneva must not be idolized either. It was not a perfect city, Calvin was not a perfect man, and its fusion of church and civil authority belonged to its century rather than to the abiding pattern of Scripture. The dictionary honors what was honorable—the faithful preaching of the Word, the right ordering of the church, the training of ministers, and the spread of the Reformed faith—while pointing, as Calvin himself did, away from the city and the man to Christ and the Scriptures. Geneva’s glory was never its own but the gospel it recovered and sent forth.

etymology: From Helvetic (Swiss, from Latin Helvetia) and consensus formula (an agreed statement); a Swiss Reformed confessional document of 1675.
biblical_def: The Helvetic Consensus Formula (Latin Formula Consensus Helvetica) is a Swiss Reformed confessional document drawn up in 1675, chiefly by the theologians Heidegger, Turretin, and Gernler, to defend the orthodox Reformed faith against the novel teachings issuing from the French Academy of Saumur. It addressed three matters especially: it upheld the verbal inspiration and providential preservation of the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, including the vowel points, against those who would loosen confidence in the received text; it defended particular, definite atonement against the hypothetical universalism of Amyraut, who taught that Christ died for all conditionally; and it maintained the immediate imputation of Adam’s sin against those who softened original sin. The Formula thus stands as a high-water mark of Reformed scholastic precision, contending earnestly for the purity of the gospel of grace at a time when subtle compromises were creeping in. The dictionary honors the Helvetic Consensus Formula as a faithful, if rigorous, defense of Reformed orthodoxy—particularly its clear witness to definite atonement and the authority of the received text—while noting that its insistence on the inspiration of the very vowel points went beyond what later Reformed confession has required, the vowel points being a later scribal aid rather than part of the original autographs. The document was never as widely received as the great confessions, and fell into disuse within a few generations, but it remains a valuable witness to the Reformed concern to guard every part of the faith against erosion.
webster_summary: A 1675 Swiss Reformed confession defending definite atonement, the immediate imputation of Adam’s sin, and the received Hebrew text against the novel teachings of Saumur.

corruption_summary: The novelties of Saumur—hypothetical universalism and a softened original sin—were the corruption the Formula was framed to resist.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruptions the Formula resisted were the novelties issuing from the French Academy of Saumur: Amyraut’s hypothetical universalism, which taught that Christ died for all men conditionally and so loosened the Reformed doctrine of definite atonement; Placeus’s mediate imputation, which softened the immediate imputation of Adam’s sin; and a critical loosening of confidence in the received Hebrew text. The Formula contended that Christ laid down His life for the sheep, that judgment came upon all by Adam’s one offence, and that all Scripture is God-breathed.

The dictionary honors the Formula’s vigilance while marking its one excess. Its defense of particular atonement and the authority of the received text was sound and necessary; its insistence on the inspiration of the very Hebrew vowel points, however, claimed for a later scribal aid what belongs properly to the original autographs, and later Reformed confession has not required it. The document was never as widely received as the great confessions and soon fell into disuse. Yet it remains a worthy witness to the Reformed instinct to guard every doctrine of grace against subtle erosion, and a reminder that compromises which seem small at the edges threaten the whole gospel.

etymology: From Calvin, Geneva, and liturgy (Greek leitourgia, public service); the order of worship Calvin established for the church at Geneva.
biblical_def: Calvin’s Geneva Liturgy, properly The Form of Church Prayers, is the order of worship that John Calvin established for the Reformed church at Geneva, drawn in part from his earlier work among the French congregation at Strasbourg. It set forth a simple, Word-centered, reverent form of worship governed by the conviction that God is to be worshipped only as He has commanded. The service moved through confession of sin and the assurance of pardon, the singing of the psalms, prayer, the reading and preaching of the Scriptures, the prayers of intercession, and, in Calvin’s desire, the frequent celebration of the Lord’s Supper. Calvin stripped away the accumulated ceremonies, images, and inventions of the medieval mass, retaining only what Scripture warranted, and he restored congregational singing in the people’s own tongue, chiefly the metrical psalms, so that the whole congregation might worship with understanding. This liturgy shaped Reformed worship across Europe and Britain, influencing Knox’s Scottish liturgy and the wider Reformed and Presbyterian tradition. The dictionary honors Calvin’s Geneva Liturgy as a model of worship reformed by the Word—simple, reverent, intelligible, and ordered to the glory of God and the edification of the people. It embodies the principle that the church does not invent its worship but receives it from God, offering Him not the devices of men but the prayer, praise, and preaching He has appointed.
webster_summary: The Word-centered order of worship Calvin established for Geneva—confession, psalm-singing, prayer, and preaching—stripping away medieval ceremony and shaping Reformed worship across Europe.

corruption_summary: Reformed simplicity of worship is abandoned for either bare neglect or the return of unwarranted ceremony and spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is worship reformed by the Word: simple, reverent, intelligible, and ordered by what God has commanded rather than by the inventions of men. Calvin’s liturgy stripped away the accumulated ceremonies of the medieval mass and retained only what Scripture warranted, restoring the people’s own singing and the centrality of the preached Word. Against both the dead ceremonialism it left behind and the modern drift toward entertainment and spectacle, it holds worship to its proper pattern.

Where a corruption presses, it presses from two sides. On one side stands the return of unwarranted ceremony, image, and theatrical performance that crowds out the Word and turns worship into a show; on the other stands a bare and careless neglect that strips worship not only of invention but of reverence, order, and beauty. Calvin’s liturgy avoids both: it is simple but not slovenly, reverent but not ceremonial, full of Scripture, prayer, and psalmody, ordered to the glory of God and the building up of His people. The dictionary commends it as a lasting model of worship received from God rather than devised by men.

etymology: From Reformed and worship; the manner of corporate worship recovered by the Reformation according to the regulative principle.
biblical_def: Reformed worship is the manner of corporate worship recovered by the Reformation and governed by the regulative principle—the conviction that God is to be worshipped only in the ways He has commanded in His Word, and not according to the imaginations and devices of men. Where the Lutheran and Anglican reformers retained whatever Scripture did not forbid, the Reformed churches held that whatever Scripture does not command in worship is not permitted, for the second commandment forbids will-worship and the fashioning of our own approach to God. From this principle flow the marks of Reformed worship: the centrality of the preached Word, the reading of Scripture, prayer, the singing of praise (the psalms above all), and the right administration of the two sacraments of baptism and the Lord’s Supper. It removes from worship the images, ceremonies, relics, and inventions that had accumulated over the centuries, and aims at simplicity, reverence, intelligibility, and the edification of the people, that all be done decently and in order to the glory of God. Reformed worship is God-centered rather than man-centered, ordered to His glory rather than to the worshippers’ entertainment or emotional gratification. The dictionary holds Reformed worship as the recovery of biblical worship from medieval corruption and a standing rebuke to every age’s temptation to remake worship after its own taste: the church comes not to offer God what pleases itself, but to render Him the worship He has appointed, in spirit and in truth.
webster_summary: Corporate worship recovered by the Reformation and governed by the regulative principle—Word, prayer, praise, and sacrament as God commands—simple, reverent, God-centered, free of human invention.

corruption_summary: Worship is remade after human taste—by the return of images and ceremony, or by entertainment-driven, man-centered performance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative principle: God is to be worshipped only as He has commanded, not as men devise. Reformed worship removed the images, ceremonies, and inventions of the medieval church on the warrant of the second commandment, which forbids fashioning our own approach to God. Against every age’s impulse to remake worship after its own taste, the church is bound to render God the worship He has appointed—Word, prayer, praise, and sacrament—in spirit and in truth.

The corruption presses from two directions. On one side is the return of unwarranted ceremony, image, and ritual, the very things the Reformation cast out, dressing worship in human invention. On the other is the modern entertainment model, which remakes worship as a performance aimed at the worshippers’ emotional gratification and the crowd’s preferences, measuring success by attendance and feeling rather than faithfulness. The dictionary names both as departures from biblical worship. Reformed worship is God-centered, simple, reverent, and ordered by His command; it comes not to please men but to glorify God, who has told us how He will be worshipped and forbidden us to add to or diminish from it.

etymology: From Reformed and confessions (Latin confessio, a public acknowledgment of faith); the doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches.
biblical_def: The Reformed confessions are the doctrinal standards by which the Reformed churches have publicly confessed their faith—corporate, ordered statements of what the church believes the Scriptures to teach, framed to confess the truth, exclude error, instruct the people, and bind the church’s teachers. They are subordinate standards, always beneath Scripture and answerable to it, yet binding upon those churches that receive them. The chief among them include, in the Continental tradition, the Three Forms of Unity—the Belgic Confession, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Canons of Dort; the Second Helvetic Confession; and in the British tradition the Westminster Confession of Faith with its Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and, for the Reformed Baptists, the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith, which largely follows Westminster except on baptism, the church, and the civil magistrate. These confessions arose in the heat of the Reformation and the controversies that followed, hammered out by assemblies of godly and learned men to set forth the recovered gospel of grace with clarity and to guard it against Rome, against Arminianism, and against every error. The dictionary honors the Reformed confessions as faithful summaries of biblical truth and precious instruments of the church’s unity, teaching, and stability, while always holding them in their proper place: they bind the conscience only as they agree with Scripture, which alone is the supreme and infallible rule, and they are honored not as a rival to the Word but as the church’s ordered confession of what the Word teaches.
webster_summary: The doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches—Belgic, Heidelberg, Dort, Westminster, the 1689, and others—subordinate to Scripture yet binding on the churches that receive them.

corruption_summary: Confessions are either exalted above Scripture or despised as needless, against their proper place as subordinate standards.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right place of confessions: subordinate to Scripture, yet binding on the churches that receive them. An anti-creedal spirit, common in the age, despises all confessions as needless human additions and boasts “no creed but the Bible”—forgetting that everyone has a confession, whether written and accountable or unwritten and hidden, and that the church is commanded to hold fast the form of sound words and to confess the faith with the mouth.

The opposite error exalts the confession to the place of Scripture, treating the standard as itself infallible and binding the conscience absolutely. The dictionary holds the Reformed balance. The confessions are faithful summaries of biblical truth, precious for unity, teaching, and stability, and rightly binding on the churches that adopt them and the teachers who subscribe them; but they are subordinate standards, beneath the Word and answerable to it, binding the conscience only as they agree with Scripture, which alone is the supreme and infallible rule of faith and life. They are the church’s ordered confession of what the Word teaches, not a rival to the Word itself.

etymology: From Reformed and liturgy (Greek leitourgia, public service); the ordered form of Reformed corporate worship.
biblical_def: Reformed liturgy is the ordered form of corporate worship in the Reformed churches—the shape and sequence of the elements God has appointed, arranged for the edification of the people and the glory of God. Though “liturgy” is sometimes thought to belong only to elaborate and ceremonial traditions, every church has a liturgy, an order of worship, whether thoughtfully framed or carelessly assumed; the question is not whether to have an order but what order to keep. Reformed liturgy, governed by the regulative principle, arranges only those elements Scripture warrants: the call to worship, confession of sin and assurance of pardon, the reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, the singing of praise, the confession of the faith, the offering, the benediction, and the right administration of the sacraments. Many Reformed churches have followed a dialogical pattern—God speaks in His Word and the people answer in prayer and praise, a covenantal conversation of revelation and response. The aim throughout is reverence, order, intelligibility, and the building up of the saints, that all things be done decently and in order. The dictionary commends a thoughtful Reformed liturgy against two errors: the bare carelessness that despises all order as “dead form” and so worships God haphazardly, and the elaborate ceremonialism that adds to worship what God has not commanded. A right liturgy is simply the wise and reverent ordering of the worship God has appointed, so that His people may draw near to Him with understanding, in spirit and in truth.
webster_summary: The ordered form of Reformed corporate worship—the Scripture-warranted elements wisely arranged for reverence, order, and edification, often as a covenantal dialogue of God’s Word and the people’s response.

corruption_summary: Order in worship is either despised as dead form or swollen into ceremonialism beyond what God commands.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that order in worship is biblical and necessary—“let all things be done decently and in order”—and that every church has a liturgy whether it acknowledges one or not. The careless spirit that despises all order as “dead form” does not escape liturgy but only keeps a thoughtless one, often worshipping God haphazardly and to little edification. A wise Reformed liturgy arranges the elements God has appointed for reverence and the building up of His people.

The opposite corruption swells the liturgy into elaborate ceremonialism, adding to worship rites and forms God has not commanded and burdening the conscience with human inventions. The dictionary holds the Reformed mean between the two: an order shaped by the regulative principle, containing only the elements Scripture warrants, yet arranged with care, reverence, and intelligibility, often as a covenantal dialogue in which God speaks in His Word and the people answer in confession, prayer, and praise. True liturgy is not a cage but a path—the wise ordering of the worship God appointed, that His people may draw near with understanding and godly fear.

etymology: From the Westminster Assembly and directory (a guide of directions, rather than a fixed prescribed form); the Assembly’s guide for worship.
biblical_def: The Westminster Directory for the Public Worship of God is the guide for worship produced by the Westminster Assembly in 1645, intended to replace the Book of Common Prayer in the churches of England, Scotland, and Ireland. Unlike a prescribed liturgy that fixes every word to be read, the Directory offered directions—a framework of guidance for the ordering and conduct of worship, leaving the minister to lead in his own words within scriptural bounds. It set forth directions for the assembling of the congregation, public prayer, the reading and preaching of the Word (with a notable treatment of the right method of preaching), the administration of baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the sanctification of the Lord’s Day, the solemnization of marriage, the visitation of the sick, burial of the dead, and the singing of psalms. It embodied the Puritan and Reformed conviction that worship is to be governed by the Word and conducted with reverence, simplicity, and edification, free from the imposed forms and ceremonies the Puritans judged unwarranted. The dictionary honors the Westminster Directory as a faithful expression of Reformed worship in the British tradition, a companion to the Westminster Confession and Catechisms, embodying the regulative principle in practice. It stands as a model of worship directed rather than dictated—ordered by Scripture, reverent in conduct, centered on the Word and prayer and psalmody—and remains a valued guide in the Presbyterian and broader Reformed churches that trace their heritage to the Assembly.

corruption_summary: Worship is either bound again by imposed forms or left to careless disorder, against the Directory’s ordered freedom under the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is worship directed by Scripture rather than dictated by imposed forms or left to careless disorder. The Directory replaced the fixed prescriptions of the Prayer Book with a framework of scriptural guidance, trusting the minister to lead in his own words within godly bounds. It embodies the regulative principle: worship ordered by the Word, reverent in conduct, centered on prayer, preaching, and psalmody, free of unwarranted ceremony.

Where a corruption presses, it presses from two directions, as it did in the seventeenth century and does still. On one side stands the imposition of fixed liturgical forms upon the conscience, the very burden the Puritans labored to remove; on the other stands a careless disorder that, despising all guidance, conducts worship without reverence, preparation, or edification. The dictionary commends the Directory’s wise middle path: not a script that binds, nor a vacuum that breeds chaos, but ordered freedom under the Word—reverent, simple, intelligible worship, directed by Scripture and conducted to the glory of God and the building up of His people.

etymology: From Scottish and psalter (a metrical version of the Psalms for singing); the metrical psalter of the Church of Scotland, chiefly the 1650 edition.
biblical_def: The Scottish Psalter is the metrical version of the Book of Psalms long used in the worship of the Church of Scotland and the wider Presbyterian world, the most famous edition being that of 1650. It renders the whole Psalter into metrical English verse so that the congregation may sing the inspired songs of Scripture, set to common meters that fit a body of well-loved psalm tunes. The 1650 Psalter arose from the Reformation conviction, embodied in the Westminster Standards, that the praise of God in worship should be drawn from His own Word, and supremely from the Psalms He gave for that very purpose. Its verse is plain, sturdy, and reverent, prizing faithfulness to the text above poetic ornament; generations of Scots and their descendants across the world have sung it in kirk and home, in covenant and persecution, at communion seasons and at the graveside. Among its treasures is the beloved metrical Twenty-third Psalm, “The Lord’s my Shepherd, I’ll not want.” The dictionary honors the Scottish Psalter as a noble fruit of Reformed worship and a chief vehicle of the practice of psalm-singing—the rendering of God’s own praises back to Him in the words He inspired. Whether or not a church holds to exclusive psalmody, the Scottish Psalter stands as a witness that the Psalms are given to be sung, that congregational praise should be rich in Scripture, and that the simplest faithful verse, sung from the heart, is fitter worship than the most polished invention of men.

corruption_summary: Congregational praise drifts from the inspired Psalms toward shallow human composition, losing the riches of singing God’s own Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the singing of God’s own Word in the praise of His people. The Scottish Psalter embodies the Reformation conviction that the Psalms are given to be sung, and that congregational praise should be rich in Scripture. Against a modern worship that has largely abandoned the Psalter for shallow and repetitive human compositions, the Scottish Psalter stands as a witness to the depth, breadth, and faithfulness of singing the inspired songs God Himself provided.

The dictionary commends the Scottish Psalter without binding the conscience to exclusive psalmody, which faithful Reformed believers have held in differing ways. Whether a church sings only psalms or psalms alongside sound hymns, the principle the Psalter teaches stands: the praise of God should be saturated with His Word, reverent, and substantial, not thin and man-centered. The plainest faithful verse of a metrical psalm, sung from the heart in the words God inspired, is fitter and richer worship than the most polished invention of men; the loss of psalm-singing is a real impoverishment of the church’s praise.

etymology: From Greek psaltērion (a stringed instrument, then the collection of psalms sung to it), through Latin psalterium; the Book of Psalms, especially in a form arranged for singing.
biblical_def: The Psalter is the Book of Psalms—the inspired hymnbook of the people of God—especially as arranged for singing in worship. The hundred and fifty psalms, gathered into five books, were given by God through David and other inspired writers as the songbook of Israel and of the church, embracing the whole range of the believer’s experience before God: praise and lament, confession and thanksgiving, trust and complaint, instruction and prophecy. The Psalter is uniquely the Word of God to us and the words of God’s people back to Him, for in it God has given us inspired language with which to speak to Him. It is profoundly Christ-centered: the Lord Jesus is everywhere in the Psalms, who sang them, fulfilled them, and quoted them upon the cross; many psalms speak directly of His suffering, His resurrection, His kingship, and His priesthood. The church has sung the Psalter from the beginning, and the Reformation, recovering congregational praise, gave the Psalms back to the people in metrical versions for singing. The dictionary honors the Psalter as the divinely given treasury of praise and prayer, calling it, with the old divines, an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. Whether sung exclusively or alongside sound hymns, the Psalter ought to hold a central and cherished place in the worship and devotion of the church: God has given His people a songbook, breathed out by His Spirit, and to neglect it is to leave untouched one of the richest stores of grace He has provided.

corruption_summary: The Psalter is neglected in the church’s praise, its inspired riches abandoned for thin and man-centered song.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the central place of the Psalter in the worship and devotion of the church. God has given His people an inspired songbook, breathed out by His Spirit, embracing the whole life of the soul before Him and full of Christ from end to end. Against a modern church that has largely abandoned the Psalms for repetitive and shallow compositions, the dictionary calls believers back to the treasury God Himself provided, that their praise might be deep, scriptural, and Christ-centered.

The neglect of the Psalter is a real impoverishment. In it the afflicted find words for their grief, the joyful for their praise, the penitent for their confession, and all the saints a language for prayer that the Spirit Himself inspired. Whether a church sings the Psalms exclusively or alongside sound hymns, to leave the Psalter unsung is to leave untouched one of the richest stores of grace in the Scriptures. The dictionary commends the recovery of psalm-singing as the Reformation recovered it: the people of God lifting back to Him, in the words He gave, the praises He delights to hear.

etymology: From musical (of music) and worship; the singing of praise to God as an element of corporate worship.
biblical_def: Musical worship is the singing of praise to God as an appointed element of corporate worship—the congregation lifting its voice in song to the Lord. Scripture everywhere commands and commends the praise of God in song: the people are to sing unto the Lord a new song, to come before His presence with singing, to teach and admonish one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in their hearts to the Lord. The chief instrument of musical worship is the human voice of the gathered congregation; the emphasis of the New Testament falls on the heart and the understanding—singing “with the spirit” and “with the understanding,” making melody “in your heart to the Lord.” The substance of the church’s song should be the Word of God, the Psalms above all and whatever is faithful to Scripture, that the word of Christ may dwell in the people richly. Reformed believers have differed on questions of exclusive psalmody and the use of instruments, holding these in good conscience within the bounds of the regulative principle. But the great matter is plain: God is to be praised in song by His people, with reverence, understanding, and a true heart, to His glory and not for the gratification of the singers. The dictionary commends musical worship as a sweet and serious duty and privilege, and warns against the modern reduction of it to performance and emotional stimulation—a band before an audience rather than a congregation before God. The end of all musical worship is the praise of God, sung from the heart, in truth.

corruption_summary: Sung praise is reduced to performance and emotional stimulation—a band before an audience rather than a congregation before God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that musical worship is the congregation’s praise of God, sung with the heart and the understanding, its substance the Word of God. The chief instrument is the people’s own voice, and the end is the glory of God, not the gratification of the singers. Against the modern reduction of worship music to a performance staged for an audience, the dictionary recovers the biblical pattern: the gathered people lifting their voices together to the Lord, in psalms and Scripture-faithful song, with reverence and a true heart.

The corruption is the turning of sung praise into spectacle and emotional stimulation—a skilled band before a passive audience, the lights dimmed, the volume raised, the aim being to produce a feeling rather than to praise God in spirit and truth. The dictionary names this as a departure from worship’s purpose, while leaving room for the genuine differences Reformed believers hold on exclusive psalmody and instruments. The great matter is the heart and the substance: God is praised when His people sing His Word to Him with understanding and reverence; He is not honored when worship is staged for the pleasure of men. The end of all musical worship is the praise of God, sung from the heart, in truth.
